query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An isothermal annealing treatment applied to the as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote a microstructural transformation in which the originally continuous hard (B2) phase decomposes into discrete, coherent precipitates embedded in a continuous ductile matrix (BCC or fcc). This inverted microstructure will both impede microcrack initiation and propagation and provide effective barriers to dislocation motion, thereby simultaneously improving room-temperature tensile ductility and maintaining or enhancing yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies in which a continuous hard (B2) phase interweaves with a softer phase; the many internal boundaries of the continuous hard phase act as preferred sites for microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: A single isothermal annealing treatment (for example, annealing at approximately 600°C for an extended duration such as 120 hours) applied soon after casting.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; the alloy should have a eutectic composition similar to AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 or related EHEAs that initially exhibit a continuous lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of the continuous hard phase into discrete, coherent precipitates within a continuous, more ductile matrix.
generation.mechanism: The isothermal annealing induces a phase re-partitioning where the hard phase, formerly continuous and crack-prone, breaks up into isolated precipitates. This microstructural inversion reduces stress concentrations at internal boundaries and better supports dislocation transmission, thereby lowering the likelihood of microcracking while still providing strengthening through precipitate-dislocation interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast lamellar baseline, the annealed alloy will exhibit improved tensile ductility at room temperature along with yield strengths that are maintained or slightly enhanced, due to effective dislocation pinning and reduced microcrack initiation.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-cast eutectic microstructure with continuous lamellar colonies (hard B2 phase interconnected with a softer phase) that, while strong, suffers from brittle room-temperature tensile behavior because of prevalent microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if (a) the alloy composition supports phase separation into the desired discrete precipitates, (b) the annealing temperature and duration are optimized to avoid coarsening that may degrade strength, and (c) the post-anneal processing does not reintroduce defects that compromise the new microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed annealing parameters are based on literature indications of microstructural inversion in similar alloys, the exact kinetics of phase transformation and the quantitative improvement in mechanical properties may vary with composition and processing conditions. Further experimental tuning is required to pinpoint optimal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with identical initial conditions. Subject one batch to conventional slow cooling (baseline) and the other to isothermal annealing at 600°C for 120 hours. Characterize the microstructures using SEM/TEM to assess phase connectivity and perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Quantitative microstructural analysis (phase connectivity, precipitate size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a transformation of the continuous hard phase into discrete precipitates (as evidenced by microstructural analysis) or if mechanical testing fails to show simultaneous improvement in ductility along with at least maintained yield strength relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Important details of the phase stabilities and phase transformations in this alloy remain uncertain. Based on the results, it can be assumed here that the alloy is a disordered BCC single-phase structure at 1400 °C, and that the fine-scale composition modulations observed in APT (Fig. 2(c) ) develop during the quench. However, it is possible that the alloy may be undergoing phase separation at 1400 °C. These possibilities need to be studied in future work. Condition (1), the initial “as-processed” condition, exhibited a “superalloy-like” microstructure consisting of cuboidal pockets of BCC within a continuous matrix of the ordered B2 phase. Isothermal annealing of Condition (1) at 1400 °C for 20 mins resulted in disordering of the microstructure to form a single BCC phase, followed by early stages of B2 ordering during water-quenching, resulting in Condition (2). Similar experiments have been carried out where Condition (1) samples were isothermally annealed at 1200 °C and water-quenched, with the resulting microstructure being identical to Condition (2).
